text: The interpretive history of the *bnei elohim*, the "sons of God" in Genesis 6, is among the strangest in biblical reception. The Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish work preserved most fully in Ethiopic versions and read as scripture by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, elaborated the angelic line of interpretation: the "sons of God" are fallen angels, the Watchers, who descend and corrupt humanity through forbidden teaching and miscegenation. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 may presuppose this same reading. Augustine, in *City of God*, rejected the angelic interpretation and favored the Sethite reading, in which the "sons of God" are the godly line of Seth and the daughters of men are the line of Cain. Other readers have compared Genesis 6 with ancient Near Eastern traditions in which kings and other powerful men claimed descent from gods. The flood narrative introduced in Genesis 6 also belongs to the broader Mesopotamian flood tradition, preserved most fully in the *Atrahasis* epic and in tablet XI of the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, the Utnapishtim narrative, where close parallels to the biblical flood story appear. The Hebrew word for Noah’s vessel is *tevah*, "ark" or "chest"; outside the Noah story, Scripture uses *tevah* only for the basket in which the infant Moses is set adrift on the Nile.
